articles.title: UK ministers look at quick ways to limit NDAs after Walliams allegations
articles.summary:
Government considers further curbs on non-disclosure agreements after Guardian investigation of TV personality

Ministers are looking at ways to change the law quickly to expand protections…

blocks.text: Ministers are looking at ways to change the law quickly to expand protections that stop non-disclosure agreements being used to cover up harassment or discrimination in the wake of the allegations about David Walliams.
This could involve extending measures that mean an NDA cannot be used this way to silence an employee so that it also applies to others, such as freelancers or volunteers.

Following an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News, which said Walliams used his power and status to prey on young women for sex, there have been reports that NDAs were used by an employer to silence at least one woman connected to him.
Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and a top-selling children’s author, denies any wrongdoing.

The Employment Rights Act bars NDAs being used to stop employees disclosing possible harassment or discrimination, and a recent government consultation looked at the idea of extending this protection more widely.

Such moves are expected to be speeded up after a planned meeting next week between Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, and representatives from TV and film – both of which rely heavily on freelance or contract staff – as well as publishing and sport, to discuss possible new protections.

“We are very much in the space of looking at areas that we can change quickly and without legislation if there are loopholes,” one government official said. “It is still early but extending these protections beyond employees is definitely the sort of thing we are looking at.”
Under other existing legislation, NDAs cannot be used to stop victims or witnesses of crime from giving information to certain specified bodies, for example police or regulators.
Another possible change could extend this protection so that people could speak about crimes to anyone, including the media.

Campaigners had already been pushing for greater safeguards against NDAs before the allegations about Walliams, or the conviction of Russell Brand, who was jailed on Monday for rape and sexual assault.

Zelda Perkins, a former PA to Harvey Weinstein who broke an NDA that barred her discussing the now-jailed Hollywood producer’s predatory behaviour, and has since become a leading campaigner against their misuse, said she hoped the government, led by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (DBIST), would be galvanised by the Walliams allegations.

“I have great confidence that [DBIST] are trying to create the best possible version of this,” she said. “But extending protections over harassment and discrimination beyond employees is absolutely key, and this is something where we need to keep up the pressure. The last couple of weeks have really highlighted the issues around this.”
Answering questions on Wednesday in the Commons, Nandy agreed with a Conservative question about the need to stop NDAs being abused, saying they were “central” to the problem of enforced silence.
after newsletter promotion

“I am working closely with colleagues at MoJ [Ministry of Justice],” she said. “I’ve discussed this issue with them over recent days. This will be part of the conversation that we have with the creative industries when I convene the roundtable next week.”
Separate moves, albeit in the slightly longer term, are likely to lead to a law change so that any adult who has penetrative sex with a child aged under 16 would automatically be charged with rape.

This was recommended by Louise Casey’s review into sexual abuse grooming gangs published last year, following concerns that some gang members had been able to face less serious charges by claiming they had consent for the abuse.
Lady Casey has called for swifter action to protect children and young people from high-profile men, and has urged ministers to change the law to close such loopholes.
An official said: “This was happening anyway, but there is pressure to move quickly in the light of this week. We are looking at it, but we don’t yet know when it might happen.”

articles.title: Czechia braces for massive protest as anger over government's public media reform plans boils
articles.summary: A fast-tracked bill on public media funding reform has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is due to take place in Prague on…

image.caption: 'Strike — For a free press, free media' Many in Czechia fear that the government's plans to change the way public media is funded will undermine the independence of Czech Television and Czech RadioImage: Katerina Sulova/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session late last month.
The populist coalition of Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 04:36 a.m. on October 24.
The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna Park is likely to be by far the largest to date.
What's in the bill?

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

blocks.caption: Crowds protested outside parliament while inside, the government pushed through the first reading of the controversial media funding bill on the night of October 23/24Image: Michal Kamaryt/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.
What are the objections to the bill?
Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.
Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.
CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."
There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

blocks.caption: The protests continued in the days after the late-night vote in parliamentImage: Michael Heitmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.
What has happened since the bill was fast-tracked?
The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.
CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.
Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.
It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.
Why has the reaction been so strong?

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

blocks.caption: 'For you, not for politicians' — Public broadcasters are seen by many in Czechia as cornerstones of democracyImage: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.
"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.
In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.
"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.
How has the government reacted?

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

blocks.caption: During the November 3 strike at Czech Television, hosts read the news in front of a darkened newsroomImage: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.
Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.
"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."
What are the potential risks for the government?
With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.
It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.
But this could come at a cost.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.
"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.
Could things turn violent?
Babis is aware of the danger.

blocks.caption: Public opposition to the government's plans for Czech public media are nothing new: this demonstration outside Czech Television in June called for the dismissal of Culture Minister Oto Klempir and expressed support for the country's public mediaImage: Ondrej Deml/CTK/picture alliance

blocks.text: The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."
However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.
Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

articles.title: U.S. army guard given medal by Hegseth day after Tomb of the Unknown Soldier reprimand
articles.summary: U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to the service member who scolded him and his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National…

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth has given a top award to the service member who scolded him and his staff at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier following a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery.
Pentagon said Specialist Thomas Iglesias 'correctly and respectfully' called for proper decorum
Hegseth delegation appears to be rebuked at Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

Hegseth welcomed to the Pentagon the army unit that guards the tomb and awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias with the Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Nov. 11, 2026," the Pentagon said.
On social media, Hegseth posted photos Thursday that show him pinning the award and shaking hands with a soldier. His post says: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."
We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots. https://t.co/Uk6ek6oOso—SecWar

Iglesias reprimanded Hegseth and a group of his staffers when a loud laugh was heard after they took photos at the site following a ceremony that included U.S. President Donald Trump and Vice- President JD Vance.

Video showed Hegseth taking photos on the empty steps in front of the tomb on Wednesday with his wife, Jennifer, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh.

items: Joining lawsuit, Kennedy family members say Trump's arch would be 'denigration' of JFK, RFK plots at Arlington

blocks.text: Incident follows impeachment vote

The tomb is considered to be one of the most solemn and revered war memorials in the U.S., being the final resting place of unidentified soldiers from the First World War, the Second World War and the Korean War. It has been guarded around the clock regardless of weather conditions by a soldier from the Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, also known as "The Old Guard," since 1948.
The Joint Service Commendation Medal is considered to be one of the higher awards in the military and is not typically issued to junior enlisted service members.
Republicans block impeachment push against Hegseth
Sean Parnell, the Pentagon's top spokesperson, said soon after video of the reprimand emerged that the soldier "correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."

The scolding drew attention once more to the embattled war secretary, who had survived an attempt to open impeachment proceedings. The effort was led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie and backed by Democrats, though 11 missed the vote as other Republicans rejected the effort.
LISTEN | David Smith, Guardian D.C. bureau chief, on Hegseth's future:
Front Burner28:11Pete Hegseth survives impeachment, for now

While Hegseth's critics were not successful in Tuesday's vote, Republicans may have only delayed a bid to impeach him. With Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate in January, those efforts are likely to be renewed.

Hegseth rebuked the move Tuesday in his first news conference in months, arguing that he had committed none of the high crimes required in the U.S. Constitution for his removal and framing the effort as an indictment against the nation's service members and their successes.
"This is not patriotism," Hegseth argued. "This is sabotage."

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton says ‘Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling’ after Rafah visit
articles.summary:
• F1 driver urges Israel to let aid into Gaza

  • Trip involved tour of facilities with aid workers

Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel…

blocks.text: Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel must allow aid ⁠trucks into Gaza, a day after he visited the Rafah border crossing in Egypt.

Hamilton, a seven-time ⁠world champion, arrived ⁠in ​El Arish on Tuesday, where he was briefed on how aid is prepared and coordinated before it ⁠is sent into Gaza, as he toured the Rafah crossing and the Egyptian Red Crescent’s aid warehouses.

He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire. A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

“The past ⁠three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling. It’s an ​injustice for people to ‌be denied their freedom, ‌their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated ‌as though their life matters less,” the Ferrari driver wrote on Instagram.
Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide and says its military campaign in Gaza targets Hamas militants.
Hamilton described seeing food trucks lined up and ready to go at the border that were ‌regularly held up or faced major delays.

“I saw walls stretching for miles, built to keep them in. Standing there, outside what felt like an open-air prison, all I could think about was getting in to help,” he said in the post. “At the Rafah border, I saw food trucks lined up ready to go, but they’re regularly not allowed in or face major delays. The first driver in line that I spoke to had already been waiting over 12 hours. At the nearby logistics centre, I saw the hard work of the aid workers, but I also saw what gets rejected for crazy reasons. Sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs even footballs for kids.

“Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. I know so many people feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than just watch. No excuse. I don’t want ⁠us to get used to their suffering. I don’t ​want us to ​look away.”
Allow Instagram content?

Hamilton, 41, is an ​advocate for humanitarian causes. In 2021 he founded ​Mission 44, a ‌charity that supports ​young people ​and works to improve their access to education and employment.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine,” Hamilton said last month. “I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage.”
At the crossing on Tuesday, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you”. He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Hamilton is fourth in the drivers’ championship. Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli has won the title with three races to go. The Las Vegas Grand Prix is 21 November before the Qatar Grand Prix on 29 November and the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix on 6 December.

articles.title: Putin says Russia would target foreign troops deployed to Ukraine
articles.summary:
Hardline remarks come as Ukrainian military faces disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service

Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops…
articles.byline: Pjotr Sauer and Jennifer Rankin in Dublin

blocks.text: Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.

During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.
He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine, describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.

Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.

The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.

Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.
The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.

Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.
But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.

The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords and the Budapest memorandum, which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.
Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.
“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.

EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”
Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.

More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.

According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.
Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.

The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.
Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.

articles.title: Finland bars Russian athletes from entering country over Ukraine war
articles.summary:
• Russians ‘have no business’ in country, says minister

  • Skating and cross-country skiing first to be affected

Finland says it will restrict entry to the…

blocks.text: Finland says it will restrict entry to the country for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine, potentially affecting a number of winter sports. The move follows a backlash in Finland to Russia being reinstated for the ice hockey world championships.

“As long as Russia’s war of aggression continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland,” said Elina Valtonen, the Minister for Foreign Affairs. “Their entry into the country would be a threat to Finland’s international relations. The same is true of other short-term work under visas that is not essential to Finland’s national interests.”
The Finnish foreign ministry said the measure would affect Russians competing under neutral status as well as those competing for national teams.

Finland hosts a figure skating grand prix next week and a cross-country ski World Cup this month. Both sports allow Russians to compete as “neutral athletes”. One major event to be affected is the figure skating world championships in March. Russian skaters are expected to be among the top medal contenders.

The International Skating Union (ISU) said it “has taken note of the statement today by the Finnish government related to Russian nationals entering the country and the possible consequential impact on sporting events, including the ISU figure skating world championships due to be held in Tampere, Finland, and is studying its implications”.

“ISU believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing.” The ISU added it was “seeking clarifications” from skating officials in Finland.

The change takes effect from Monday, so should not affect this week’s NHL games in Helsinki between the Seattle Kraken and Carolina Hurricanes or scheduled ski World Cup slalom races in Levi on Saturday and Sunday.

Finland is among a group of European teams to have vowed not to play against Russia at the ice hockey world championships. The men’s championships are scheduled for Germany, which is weighing up whether to go ahead with hosting.

In the longer term, Finland is due to host the European track and field championships in 2030. World Athletics, the sport’s governing body, maintains a blanket ban on Russian participation, though that is facing a legal challenge.

articles.title: Can the EU make it harder to trick consumers online?
articles.summary: The EU wants to curb subscription traps, misleading sales tactics and features that keep people scrolling. What would the proposed Digital Fairness Act change, and does it go far enough?

image.caption: The Digital Fairness Act was proposed by the Commission and is set to better protect consumers onlineImage: James Arthur Gekiere/Belga/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: You sign up for a free trial to watch a series after work. A month later, you've forgotten about it. Then you find a charge for your new 12-month subscription on your bank statement. Sound familiar? You're not alone. Now the EU wants to stop that practice.

Under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA), a company would have to remind you before the free trial ends and get your explicit agreement before it can start charging you. The proposed law would also make it easier to cancel a subscription online and require reminders before certain contracts renew automatically.
The Commission presented the proposal on Wednesday. It wants to give consumers more control over how much time and money they spend online.
"We haven't seen that kind of reform in consumer protection in the last 20 years," Agustin Reyna, director general of the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), told DW.
His organization pushed for stronger EU rules against manipulative online practices. He sees the proposal as a good starting point for tackling problems that frustrate consumers every day.

blocks.caption: EU Commissioner for the rule of law and consumer protection Michael McGrath has been pushing for the new regulationImage: Europäische Kommission

blocks.text: Ending doomscrolling and 'dark patterns'

The proposal also includes a ban on manipulative marketing tactics, so-called "dark patterns." A concrete example: You are trying to reserve a hotel room and the website claims that only three are left, a potentially false claim to pressure you into buying.

A concert ticket that gets more expensive while you're waiting in an online queue raises a different problem. The price could still go up in the process, but the seller would have to show the current price while you wait and tell you the maximum you could be asked to pay.
Online games that encourage users to spend their money to advance are also targeted. Children would no longer be able to pay to win or get to the next level of their online game.

Marketing and personalized ads would need to be clearly marked and restricted in the case of children. Consumers should get the option to switch off doomscrolling functions such as the autoplay of videos, showing one clip after the other. With these new rules, the EU wants to make apps and websites less addictive.

blocks.caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised that "Europe has the power to act: It is we who decide our rules, not big tech" (file photo from January 2026)Image: Omar Havana/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Consumer protection versus innovation?

For Christoph Busch, an academic with a focus on consumer law and digital services based at Osnabrück University in Germany, the option to opt out doesn't go far enough. He argues that a version in which consumers actively have to choose to opt into those functions would be more effective.
"But then there is always the question of proportionality," Busch said. "And I think here the European legislators are trying to balance different interests."

These competing interests are particularly visible in the gaming industry, where interest groups have warned that the proposed EU restrictions could hurt developers and leave players with fewer options to choose from.

Video Games Europe and the European Games Developer Federation called the proposal "unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate," arguing that a ban on selling children features that help them win or advance is worded so broadly that it "could cover almost any purchase in a game."
For Busch, this argument doesn't hold. "If your business model is based on addictive design features, then maybe your business model has to be reviewed," he said.

blocks.caption: The proposal still has to pass the Council and the European ParliamentImage: Alexey Vitvitsky/SNA/imago images

blocks.text: The risk of overregulation
Catalina Goanta, an associate professor of private law and technology at Utrecht University, emphasized in an interview with DW that "regulation can very easily slide into overregulation."

Even though she believes that the DFA is a solid and reasonable compromise, she argues that prohibiting dark patterns and doomscrolling altogether would be too prohibitive. Many of the issues consumers currently face could be resolved by enforcing existing regulation more effectively, she said.

She points to the fact that the EU has made a name for itself in the past by adding new rules and regulations that have made it more difficult to access the European market, especially for small online businesses.
BEUC director Agustin Reyna disagrees.
"Instead of having 27 different regulations to adhere to, companies will now only get one," Reyna said.
For him, this speaks for simplification, especially when the responsibility for compliance is shared between online influencers and the platforms they publish on.
According to the new legislation, the EU would have the possibility to impose fines of up to six percent of a company's global annual revenue should the company violate the law.
What happens next?

The European Parliament and the Council, which represents member state governments, still have to agree on the text and formally adopt it. All experts agree that in that process, changes are still very likely.

"It will be a difficult trialogue, especially in this climate of simplification and deregulation with a focus on strengthening European competitiveness," said Christoph Busch. In that climate, it is not easy to add consumer rights, he adds.

Agustin Reyna is more optimistic. "The parliament is a divided house, much more than in the past," he says. "But consumer protection is a subject that brings parties together because it brings tangible outcomes to people."

articles.title: Report of children confined in locker at Quebec school draws minister's condemnation
articles.summary: The students were allegedly placed in a metal locker as a disciplinary measure. The Education Ministry is in touch with the investigating authorities to better understand what took place.

image.caption: Education Minister Joël Arseneau said that his office is in touch with authorities to better understand what took place at the school. (Sylvain Roy Roussel/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·Updated
The students were allegedly placed in a metal locker as a disciplinary measure. The Education Ministry is in touch with the investigating authorities to better understand what took place.
Police investigation underway at school in the Laurentians, north of Montreal

Quebec's education minister has condemned the "unacceptable" disciplinary practice of confining students inside a locker, pointing to an incident that allegedly took place at a school in the Laurentians.

"Under no circumstances should students be confined to lockers," Joël Arseneau wrote on X Thursday. He stated that his office is in touch with authorities, and will take the necessary measures to shed light on the "highly problematic" practices.

A report from 98.5 issued Thursday said that police are investigating staff from a primary school in the Centre de services scolaire des Mille-Îles (CSSMI), who allegedly had shut five- to seven-year-old children in a metal locker to calm them down.
A photo of the locker obtained by Radio-Canada shows makeshift padding at the base and covering hooks near the top.
The Centre de services scolaire des Mille-Îles confirmed this is the locker that was used to confine students. (Centre de services scolaire des Mille-Îles)
When speaking with reporters, Arseneau said that he was shocked to see that this kind of practice was being used in a school — seemingly in a formalized manner.
"That's why people are reacting, this is an affront to the dignity of young people," he said. "I think it could lead to significant trauma."

The police service in Blainville, Que., confirmed that in partnership with the province’s youth protection services, they have opened an investigation into a primary school under the jurisdiction of the CSSMI.
The Blainville police were not willing to confirm that it was related to allegations about locker confinement however.
The report from 98.5 said that four employees were suspended when allegations against them surfaced.
In a letter to parents obtained by Radio-Canada, the leadership of the CSSMI wrote that once the issue was brought to their attention "they acted promptly to correct the situation."
The letter does not mention any suspensions.
The CSSMI also wrote that an investigation is underway, which limits how much information they can offer, given concerns about confidentiality.
"Please be assured that we are taking this situation very seriously and that the safety, dignity and well-being of our students remains our top priority," they wrote.
Dominique Sauvé, the president of the teachers' syndicate of the Basses-Laurentides, said on behalf of the syndicate that they believe all of the alleged facts must be fully investigated.
CBC News has reached out to Santé Quebec for comment to receive more details on the investigation, and on which school was involved, but has not heard back.
With files from Radio-Canada

articles.title: NCC mulling refrigerating downtown end of Rideau Canal
articles.summary: The CEO of the National Capital Commission (NCC) says the Crown corporation is seriously mulling artificially freezing the northern end of the Rideau Canal to make skating conditions more reliable in…

image.caption: The NCC is seriously considering artificially freezing this section of the Rideau Canal Skateway to make conditions more reliable, its CEO says. (Brian Morris/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa

The CEO of the National Capital Commission (NCC) says the Crown corporation is seriously mulling artificially freezing the northern end of the Rideau Canal to make skating conditions more reliable in the winter.
Ice conditions on 'iconic' Ottawa attraction have become less reliable due to climate change

Tobi Nussbaum told CBC Radio's Ottawa Morning on Thursday that the NCC is acting on a feasibility study that recommends using refrigeration pipes embedded in a concrete slab to help keep the skateway surface frozen, similar to refrigerated outdoor rinks.

The NCC is looking at an approximately 900-metre stretch of the canal from the Corktown Footbridge at Somerset Street W. to the National Arts Centre. Nussbaum said that section is the skateway's busiest, and also the most difficult to freeze naturally.
"We're going to pursue that," Nussbaum said. "[There's] a lot more work to do in terms of figuring out the details."
He said refrigerating that section of the canal could triple the number of days it's open for skating.
Can it truly be an Ottawa winter without the Rideau Canal skateway?

The canal, a UNESCO World Heritage Site and lynchpin of Ottawa tourism in the winter, has mostly relied on nature to freeze the skateway's 7.8-kilometre length since the NCC started clearing the ice in 1971.

Recently, the NCC commissioned a series of reports on the potential effects of climate change on the attractions and events it oversees in Ottawa-Gatineau. One study predicted the skating season on the Rideau Canal will gradually start later and end sooner, with fewer than 20 skating days by the 2050s unless greenhouse gas emissions are drastically reduced.

items: Ottawa's weather to get warmer, wetter and wilder: study
What if we refrigerated the Rideau Canal?

blocks.text: According to a detailed analysis commissioned by the NCC in 2021, the average skating season was around 46 days.
That was before 2023 when conditions were so poor that it didn't open for skating at all. The following year it opened just 10 days. Skating conditions rebounded the following two seasons.
An 'iconic symbol of Canada'
Nussbaum said it's too early to know the cost of artificially freezing a nearly kilometre-long section of the canal, though it would be expensive and beyond what the NCC could afford on its own.
But he said the investment would be well worth it.

"It's an iconic symbol of Canada," Nussbaum said. "To allow visitors from across the country to know when they come to the nation's capital, they have the option of skating, I think is really, really important."
Nussbaum said the soonest that such a system could be installed would be the early 2030s.
LISTEN | Nussbaum on the idea:
Ottawa Morning8:58Are there other ways to freeze the canal for skating every year?
With files from CBC Radio's Ottawa Morning

articles.title: Mercedes-Benz halts all further investment at German facilities
articles.summary: The announcement comes as the luxury German automaker faces increasing pressure from the works council and trade unions.

image.caption: Mercedes-Benz has long been a symbol for the German auto industryImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mercedes-Benz announced on Thursday that it was halting all further investment at its German sites for the time being.

"The executive board has jointly decided to halt all further investments in German sites," Mercedes board member Michael Schiebe said in a memo on the company's intranet that was seen by the AFP news agency.
The company is also weighing plant closures, the memo added.
The announcement comes as the luxury German automaker faces increasing pressure from the works council and the IG Metall trade union.
What else did Mercedes-Benz say?

Mercedes-Benz is "forced to examine, in concrete and detailed terms, which sites in Germany we can still afford to maintain," board of management member Britta Seeger said in an interview published on the company's intranet.
"We all want to avoid plant closures at all costs," she added. "Unfortunately, however, we must now pursue this option in more concrete terms."
Shiebe, the company's chief production officer, said the current cost structures meant it is not possible to invest in Germany.
German labour costs are sometimes five times higher than at plants in Eastern Europe, where administrative costs are also similarly much cheaper.
Schiebe had recently announced that two plants in Germany would have to close unless costs were reduced.

articles.title: Pentagon backs war memorial guard who reprimanded Hegseth's group
articles.summary: The guard told the defence secretary and his companions to maintain an atmosphere of "silence and respect" during a Veterans Day visit.

blocks.text: The Pentagon has given its backing to a US Army guard who reprimanded a group that included US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Arlington National Cemetery.
A video of the Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
The footage showed the army sentinel on duty stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored - and will always honor - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."
On Thursday, he presented an award to the soldier who reprimanded his group.

Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026," the Pentagon said in a statement.
In a post on X showing the soldier, Hesgeth said: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."
The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.
The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.
A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.
It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.

articles.title: What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?
articles.summary: The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

image.caption: Delegations from Russia and Ukraine held US-mediated talks in Abu DhabiImage: Altaf Qadri/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.
The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."
How significant is the prisoner swap?
Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.
"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."
A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.
Russia, Ukraine exchange prisoners as talks end
Empty diplomacy without a real breakthrough?

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.
Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."
Experts: chances for Russia-Ukraine ceasefire low as things currently stand

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.
Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

blocks.caption: Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, briefed journalists during the talks between Russia and UkraineImage: Altaf Qadri/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Redrawing borders to make Putin feel like a winner?

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."
Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.
"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.
Putin demands large swaths of Ukrainian territory

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.
"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.
Is Trump trying to end the war in Ukraine, or helping Putin win it?
Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.
What next after Abu Dhabi?

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.
Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Hungary eases abortion restrictions in women's rights overhaul
articles.summary: The reforms mark a break the the conservative policies of former PM Viktor Orban. The controversial "heartbeat regulation" is to be scrapped and women are to be better protected against violence.

image.caption: Peter Magyar said the heartbeat regulation had not led to a decline in pregnanciesImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.
Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.
Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.
The changes proposed by the new government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar are a significant break with the conservative policies of his predecessor Viktor Orban.
The country also plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention, a treaty aimed at preventing violence against women and domestic violence.
Hungary to end controversial 'fetal heartbeat' policy

Hungarian law allows for most abortions to be performed up to 12 weeks, and up to 24 weeks in cases of severe developmental abnormalities. Until now, women were required to have a medical provider show them evidence of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly understood as the so-called "fetal heartbeat," before deciding whether to have an abortion.
The controversial 2022 policy had received widespread criticism from doctors and women’s rights groups as being cruel and humiliating. It will now be scrapped.
The policy had not led to a decline in abortions and according to Magyar, had raised "serious bioethical questions."
The second major change is that emergency contraception will be available without prescription.

Further measures include changing the criminal code aimed at better protecting women, including making the misuse of intimate images a criminal offense and strengthening the treatment of victims of domestic violence during criminal proceedings.
What is the Istanbul Convention?

Hungary also plans to ratify an international treaty on the protection of women which most other EU members have long ratified. The Istanbul Convention came into force in 2014 and, among other things, requires rape to be criminalized based on the absence of freely given consent.
"We are making it clear that sexual acts can only ⁠take ​place with the voluntary consent of the other party," ​Magyar said.
The government of his predecessor Orban had opposed the treaty, arguing that it promoted what it described as "gender ideology."
"We are making a clear and accountable commitment to putting an end to the era of inaction," Magyar said in a Facebook video.
Among the EU’s other members, only Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovakia have not yet ratified the convention.

The Istanbul Convention is a treaty by the Council of Europe, an international organization that promotes human rights and the rule of law across Europe and includes more countries than the member of the EU.

articles.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
articles.summary: Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in both Washington and Beijing, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation.
The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom.

He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into free fall this week, undone by romantic entanglements, that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement.

On Thursday he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman, alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.
His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China.
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips, which are used to power the new technology.
The company, which is still valued at nearly $4 trillion despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang has had access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President XI Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn (£109bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work at their father's firm.
He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan, he has a reputation for having incredibly high standards for his staff.

The company became a key provider of computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in direction and entered the world of AI. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing technology.
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At a recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Huang and Musk.
It was no surprise that Huang was at the top table. Companies using Nvidia's chips include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic.
In essence, Huang's customer base includes the biggest firms on the planet and they are spending plenty on Nvidia's products.
This intertwining of companies means that the negative impact being felt by Nvidia, on the stock market for example, could perhaps have wider implications on other companies and the wider economy.
Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, and that it was "very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.
Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, had backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable".

articles.title: ‘Resetting BSKE no longer in Comelec’s hands’
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections can no longer set a new date for the postponed barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) originally scheduled for Nov. 2, leaving Congress to determine when the…

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Commission on Elections (Comelec) can no longer set a new date for the postponed barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) originally scheduled for Nov. 2, leaving Congress to determine when the polls will be held.
In an interview, Comelec Chairman George Garcia said the poll body may reschedule elections within 30 days only if the postponement is declared before the scheduled election day.

He made the clarification following election lawyer Romulo Macalintal’s motion for partial reconsideration of the Supreme Court ruling upholding the constitutionality of Republic Act 12326, which extends the terms of barangay officials to five years and sets the next BSKE on Nov. 13, 2028.
Garcia said that even if the Supreme Court reverses its earlier ruling, the Comelec may no longer have the authority to set a new date for the postponed elections.

“Under the law, if an election is postponed before the scheduled election day, we may set a new date, provided that it does not exceed 30 days from the original schedule,” he said. “However, once the scheduled election day has passed, even if a decision is issued, the Comelec may no longer have the authority to set a new date.”
He said Congress would have to determine the new election schedule if the Supreme Court reverses its decision.
‘No-el in 2028 unlikely’
Meanwhile, lawyer Ralph Sarmiento, who specializes in constitutional law, said postponing the national elections in 2028 will be unlikely following the deferment of the BSKE.
He pointed out that the 1987 Constitution has fixed the schedule of the election of national officials.

“Technically, it is highly likely that postponement will not happen with respect to the presidential and national elections because there are clearer provisions in our Constitution,” he said in an interview on The STAR’s online show “Truth on the Line.”

The Constitution declares that election for president, vice president, senator and member of the House of Representatives “shall be held on the second Monday of May,” with one term of six years for president and vice president, two terms of six years each for senator, and three terms of three years each for member of the House.
Previously, Macalintal expressed fear that a no-election or “no-el” scenario might happen, warning that lawmakers may also move to defer the May 2028 national elections.
Garcia said the Comelec is preparing for the next BSKE scheduled for Nov. 13, 2028, giving assurance that election materials procured for the postponed polls have been properly secured.
He said the commission had arranged with suppliers to safeguard election materials, including pens and indelible ink, and ensure their replacement in case of damage.
On voter registration, Garcia expressed confidence that the Comelec would surpass its target of registering three million voters for the 2028 elections.
Nearly 37,000 people registered nationwide on the first day of the registration period, with the number reaching almost 80,000 in the first two days, Garcia said.
He noted that registration turnout remained high on the third day, with some registration centers, including those in shopping malls, struggling to accommodate applicants before closing time.
He attributed the turnout partly to the participation of young Filipinos, particularly those aged 17 and 18, as well as applicants seeking to transfer their registration.
Garcia also cited the demand for voter certification, which the Comelec now provides for free, as another factor drawing applicants to registration centers.– Ghio Ong

articles.title: AMLC: No flood control money in Martin’s accounts
articles.summary: An investigator of the Anti-Money Laundering Council told the Sandiganbayan that the AMLC found no record of contractors, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), or former lawmaker Zaldy…

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — An investigator of the Anti-Money Laundering Council told the Sandiganbayan that the AMLC found no record of contractors, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), or former lawmaker Zaldy Co sending money to suspended Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez when he was House speaker.

AMLC financial investigator Jan Mark Busa, who testified in Romualdez’s bail hearing, told the court that the P560.5 million worth of remittances that went to the bank account of the Leyte lawmaker were not related to flood control transactions or unlawful activities.

During the cross-examination of defense counsel Rashel Ann Pomoy, Busa said the AMLC examined 35 accounts associated with Romualdez and monitored P560.5 million worth of bank transactions from September 2022 to March 2025.
Asked if it would be correct that the AMLC did not have findings that these transactions were related to flood control projects, Busa answered in the affirmative.
The investigation, Busa said, covered 1,951 financial transactions of Romualdez from 2022 to 2025.
He also said there “appears to be a huge disparity” between the inflow of money in Romualdez’s accounts and the P7.4-billion plundered money alleged by ombudsman prosecutors.
Busa also testified that there was no AMLC record of Romualdez sending money to Golden Pheasant, the company allegedly used by the lawmaker to purchase a property in South Forbes Park in Makati City.
Moreover, there are no records of Romualdez sending money to OMLAW, Samchan or lawyer Jose Paras.
Judge scolds BJMP over changing testimony

Third Division chairperson Associate Justice Karl Miranda scolded a Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) warden over inconsistencies in her testimony on the access granted to Romualdez’s personal staff at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas.

During the bail hearing, Supt. Maria Lourdes Pacion said that Romualdez’s personal staff, Arvin de Guzman, was allowed to set up the lawmaker’s CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine at night.

Miranda, however, pointed out that this is contrary to Pacion’s earlier testimony that De Guzman was only allowed inside the facility during visiting hours, from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., although exceeding at times.
“You’re here to tell us the truth. Stop changing the story. Just stick to one, which is the truth,” Miranda said.

Pacion said she allowed De Guzman to assist with the CPAP machine because Romualdez was not mentally stable and required continued medical care, which includes regular blood pressure monitoring, uninterrupted access and compliance with his prescribed medications, and consistent nightly use of the breathing apparatus.
However, Miranda said it seems the BJMP is giving special consideration to Romualdez by allowing him a personal assistant. Miranda said it should be the BJMP personnel attending to Romualdez’s needs.
DOJ: Over P866 million in flood money returned
More than P866 million allegedly stolen from anomalous flood control projects have been recovered by the government, the Department of Justice (DOJ) reported.
A total of P866,381,500 has been “returned to the DOJ and deposited to the Bureau of Treasury,” the agency said in its one-year accomplishment report yesterday.
The current total increased by P25 million from the P841,381,500 restituted amount last July.
It did not provide a breakdown of where the funds came from.

However, DOJ Senior Undersecretary Raul Vasquez noted that “the last one came from Henry Alcantara,” which he said was given in “cold cash,” while restitution by former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) undersecretary Roberto Bernardo was “continuous.” – Ghio Ong

articles.title: Sri Lanka: Rights groups sound alarm over proposed anti-terror law
articles.summary: The Sri Lankan government is looking to replace a controversial anti-terror law but critics say the new one is just as bad.

image.caption: The government argues a robust anti-terrorism law is needed to address the increasingly complex activities of extremist groupsImage: Eranga Jayawardane/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: For 46-year-old Ganesan (name changed) from Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka, any discussion of terrorism brings back memories of his two-year-old daughter, who was killed in the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks. She was one of 270 people who lost their lives in a series of coordinated bombings targeting three churches and three luxury hotels across the island nation.
The attacks were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Over 500 people were injured.
Ganesan's daughter was killed in an attack on the Zion Church in Batticaloa.
But Ganesan remains skeptical when asked about the new counterterrorism bill pushed by the government in Sri Lanka.
"Laws against terrorism are necessary to prevent terrorist attacks, but they should not target the innocent or suppress human rights," he told DW.
The administration led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and his National People's Power faction

has proposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA) as a replacement for the existing Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). The PTA has many critics who claim that the contentious law has enabled arbitrary detention and the torture of detainees for decades.
The government argues that a robust anti-terrorism law is needed to address the increasingly complex local and international activities of extremist groups.
What do rights groups say about the new bill?

But rights groups are now also sharply criticizing the new bill. Activist argue that the changes will not bring about any improvement, warning that the draft features an overly broad definition of terrorism, provides inadequate judicial oversight, and grants extensive powers to law enforcement authorities. Activists also warn that the proposed law has only limited safeguards against official abuse.

The bill, for instance, allows security forces to stop, search and question individuals on the basis of "reasonable suspicion," enter and search premises, and seize items on suspicion of them being linked to an offense under the terrorism act.

blocks.caption: President Anura Kumara Dissanayake's government is replacing the contentious Prevention of Terrorism Act [FILE: September 22, 2024]Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: "The definition of the term 'terrorism' in the bill as presently drafted is highly problematic. The term is unclear, and its meaning has not been clearly defined," Visakesa Chandrasekaram, a film director and human rights lawyer, told DW.
"Such lack of clarity in the law may result in violations of the fundamental rights of the people," he added.

Chandrasekaram also pointed out that the bill would confer police powers on the military, which is neither trained to investigate criminal offenses nor equipped to protect the rights of people targeted in such investigations.
This, he warned, could lead to the "militarization" of the law enforcement process.
Is the new law just PTA all over again?
Dhanushka Silva, a lawyer, said the proposed law is not much different from the existing one.
"The present government pledged to repeal the PTA in their 2024 election manifesto. But now the government seems to replace it with a new act that is a replica of the PTA," he told DW.
Silva believes the new bill, PSTA, could be misused to suppress democratic freedoms and muzzle dissent and free speech.
Under Section 9 of the PSTA, even posts or statements made on social media could be subject to scrutiny due to the broad definition of terrorism-related offenses in the bill, he explained.
The section further suggests that individuals who share content deemed to be a terrorism offense could face up to 15 years of rigorous imprisonment, according to the the lawyer.
"This is a big blow to freedom of speech in a democratic society like ours," he said.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has also called on the government to ensure that the bill is consistent with international human rights law.
It noted that the PSTA, despite containing some additional safeguards and improvements on previous drafts, reproduces a number of shortcomings in the PTA and other, older counter-terrorism bills.
The legislation "should include robust safeguards against torture, ill-treatment, enforced disappearance and coercive interrogation," it said in a statement.
Government spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa, however, rejected the allegations by rights activists and insisted that the new law would not compromise civil liberties and press freedom.

blocks.caption: The 2019 Easter Sunday attacks targeted three churches and three luxury hotels across Sri Lanka [FILE: April 21, 2020]Image: Eranga Jayawardena/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Calls for Colombo to uphold human rights commitments
Passing the new counterterrorism legislation could also have economic and foreign policy ramifications for Sri Lanka.
The United Nations, which has repeatedly urged Colombo to repeal the PTA, has called for further revisions to the proposed PSTA.

The European Union has likewise urged Sri Lanka to uphold its international human rights obligations if it wishes to continue benefiting from the bloc's Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+), which grants preferential access to the EU market to eligible developing countries.
Failure to meet these requirements could result in the suspension of GSP+ preferences, likely to trigger significant economic penalties for the country.
During a parliamentary debate on November 12, Speaker Jagath Wickramaratne said that some provisions of the proposed law were inconsistent with the constitution.
The legislation was also challenged before the Supreme Court, which outlined several amendments and said Parliament could pass the measure once the changes were made.
Parliament has yet to set a date for a vote.
